request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

History of Present Illness:
The patient, a 10-year, 10-month-old male neutered Shih Tzu, was admitted for further examination of a peracute onset of lethargy and left-sided circling. The general physical examination was normal. Neurological examination revealed circling to the left, decreased proprioceptive positioning of the right thoracic and pelvic limbs, and a decreased menace response on the right side. Routine hematology and serum biochemistry were normal. Urine-specific gravity, urine chemistry dipstick analysis, sediment examination, and urine culture were all unremarkable. Assessment of NIBP using Doppler identified a systolic pressure of 170 mmHg. Fibrinogen, PT, aPTT, and D-dimer were all within normal limits. TEG analysis revealed a shortened R time and SP on citrated plasma. MRI scan of the brain under general anesthesia showed an extensive intra-axial, focal, well-demarcated lesion affecting the cerebral gray matter extending from the left frontal lobe to the rostral aspects of the left temporal lobe. The lesion was T2W and FLAIR hyperintense compared to normal gray matter and T1W hypointense. There was evidence of mild mass effect, and there was no contrast enhancement.

Hospital Course:
The patient was closely monitored, and no underlying cause for the ischemic stroke could be identified. The dog improved with time and was discharged from the hospital 72 h after admission. The dog made a near to full recovery within 14 days and was neurologically normal at re-assessment five months later.

Medications:
N/A

Follow-up Care:
None necessary at this time.

Signed,
[Physician Name]

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The patient is a dog, but the task is to assign an ICD-10-AM category to the episode as described. The condition is an ischemic stroke: a cerebral infarction with an acute onset and a focal left cerebral lesion, with no identified cause (no embolism or thrombosis was established). The ICD-10 category for cerebral infarction is I63.

I63 is the best fit for ischemic stroke in the circulatory chapter. I64 (stroke, not specified as haemorrhage or infarction) is less appropriate because the imaging and the summary both indicate infarction.

CODE: I63
